fetched_contents.text: Palpable breast lumps: An age-based approach to evaluation and diagnosis Abstract A palpable breast lump is a common presentation of breast disease to a general practitioner. Fortunately, investigation of most of these lumps will lead to a benign diagnosis. It is essential to have a clear and systematic approach when investigating a palpable breast lump to avoid over investigation with the resultant increase in healthcare cost and anxiety. This article will discuss an approach to evaluating and diagnosing a palpable breast lump in the primary care setting. Keywords: breast lump, palpable, primary care, diagnostic guide, age-based approach Introduction Breast lumps are common in general practice. More than 25% of women are affected by breast disease during their lifetime, the vast majority of whom will complain of a new breast lump.1 Fortunately, most of these will be benign, with breast cancer only diagnosed in 10% of new breast lumps.2 It is essential to have an approach to investigating breast lumps that is simple to follow, limiting over investigation and preventing the misdiagnosis of malignant breast lesions. The risk of a breast lump representing a breast cancer increases with age, with a 1/204 (0.49%) chance of breast cancer for a woman in her thirties, compared with 1/28 (3.54%) chance for a woman in her sixties.3 The risk of a breast lump being malignant in adolescence is exceedingly rare.4 Triple assessment With very few exceptions, every patient who presents with a breast lump needs to undergo a triple assessment. The triple assessment consists of a history and physical examination, some form of breast imaging and a biopsy. It is the gold standard in breast cancer diagnosis, with a positive predictive value of 100% if all three modalities are positive for breast cancer.5 History and physical examination A full history, as with any other patient, is important. When dealing with a breast complaint, appropriate history taking helps to risk-stratify the patient by identifying known factors associated with breast disease. This includes a detailed family history of cancer. A relevant family history in a patient with a breast lump includes asking about breast, ovarian, prostate, colon, pancreatic and other malignancies associated with specific genetic mutations, for example, BRCA 1 and 2, TP53, PALB 3, etc. Online risk calculators such as the Tyrer–Cuzick model (International Breast Cancer Intervention Study [IBIS], London, United Kingdom) help to individualise patient’s genetic risk.6 Information with regard to the patient’s oestrogen window (age of menarche and menopause), exogenous hormone exposure (use of contraceptives, hormone replacement therapy or fertility treatment), childbearing and breastfeeding history and lifestyle risk factors such as smoking, obesity and alcohol consumption further assist in the risk stratification process. It is also important to note any previous breast pathology or concerns. The physician should try to gain as much information as possible about the current complaint by enquiring about the characteristics of the lump; location and duration of the lump; changes in size; variation with menstrual cycle; pain, swelling or erythema; and nipple discharge or inversion. A systematic examination of the breast must be undertaken. A visual inspection needs to be completed with the patient in a sitting and supine position. Observation must be made of the overall breast size, shape and symmetry. The best way is to ask the patient to position the ipsilateral hand under the head while the breast is examined. The examiner must use their finger pads, usually with the hand in a slightly cupped position. There are different techniques to examine a breast, but the most common methods used are the radial ‘wagon wheel’ method, the vertical strip method and the concentric circle method.7 Being thorough and consistently using the same approach is more important than a specific technique to achieve the best results, and different methods can be used on opposite breasts to make the examination ergonomically easier. The overall consistency of the breast is documented soft, firm or nodular. The position of any masses or tender lesions is observed in relation to the location in a conventional quadrant or clock face configuration. Essential findings to document would be characteristics of any abnormalities, including size, shape, texture, mobility, tenderness and approximate depth. Lastly, the examiner needs to examine the nipple–areola complex (NAC). The tissue around the NAC must be palpated to assess any abnormalities, including nipple discharge. The presence of a nipple discharge is noticed while the tissue around the areola is firmly pressed down. An axillary and supraclavicular fossa examination are part of a breast exam, and any palpable abnormalities in these areas must be documented. Should the clinician have difficulty in finding the reported lump, he or she can ask the patient to indicate where the lump was felt and in what position they were at the time the lump was felt. Some subtle changes may only be apparent if a patient is in a specific position, such as turned on the side or sitting up. Finding a breast lump with axillary adenopathy would raise high suspicion of breast cancer and needs a thorough assessment. Imaging Radiological assessment of the breast is essential and commonly consists of either an ultrasound, mammogram or both. Another radiological test that is less typically used is a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast. A breast MRI is usually carried out for one of the following reasons: to follow up high-risk patients with dense breast tissue or to obtain more information in selected patients diagnosed with breast cancer. It is advisable that a breast MRI should only be requested by a specialist. In women under 35 years, breast ultrasound would be the imaging modality of choice. fetched_contents.text: Paying for Care The Access to Care (ATC) team are certified application counselors who can answer questions about enrolling in health insurance. They are available to meet virtually or in-person to provide step-by-step assistance to enroll and pay for care. Our team also connects residents with other vital resources. Have a question? Schedule a time to meet with ATC, today! Insurance We accept Medicare and HUSKY Health (Medicaid) as well as many commercial health insurance plans. With insurance, the charges for your visit are based upon many factors, such as services provided, your insurance status, your insurance policy’s benefits, deductibles, co-pays or co-insurance fees. We recommend that you review your health insurance plan booklet or call your insurance company representative before you visit, to make sure you understand your specific policy benefits and provider network requirements. It’s important to know who you have chosen as your Primary Care Physician, and to update that if necessary before your appointment. Failure to follow your plan requirements may result in greater out-of-pocket expenses for you, so it’s really important to stay up-to-date with your insurance company’s policies. Uninsured or Underinsured If you do not have insurance, or you’re underinsured (your insurance doesn’t cover everything you need it to), CHC offers a Sliding Fee Discount program, which provides reduced rates for those who qualify. If you qualify, visit fees will be based on a sliding scale using income and household size. Prescriptions If you have concerns about paying for your prescriptions, we have a Pharmacy Assistance Program that may be able to help. Please talk to your provider about your concerns, and they can connect you with that program. As a Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC), CHC offers discounts based on income in accordance with federal poverty guidelines and household size. Our on-site Patient Services Associates (PSAs), the Patient Accounts/Billing Department, and our Access to Care (ATC) team can help determine if you qualify. You can qualify even if you are insured. Please note that Sliding Scale Fee is not insurance, and qualifying for Sliding Scale Fee at CHC only covers services accessed at CHC. Practical reassurance and next steps for the patient

The best way to explain the situation clearly to a provider is to say: “I found a lump that hurts, and I’m worried it might be something serious. I want to know what it could be and what I should do next.” That is direct, honest, and gives the provider enough context to ask focused questions. The evidence supports that most lumps are benign and that evaluation is usually needed to distinguish benign from malignant causes [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. It also suggests that a provider will ask about the lump’s characteristics, duration, and any changes, which helps build a clearer picture of what is happening [N1-F1].

During the evaluation, the patient should ask for the provider to explain whether the lump is likely cancerous or not, and whether more tests are needed [N1-F1]. The evidence also says that a provider may order imaging and biopsies when necessary, so it is reasonable to ask, “What tests will you do?” and “What do those results mean?” [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The patient should also ask about whether the lump is moving, whether it has changed in size or shape, and whether there are any red flags that would require urgent care [N2-R1][N2-F2]. A practical next step is to ask the provider to explain the findings in plain language and to clarify whether follow-up is needed.

If the provider is unavailable, the patient should follow up as soon as possible. The evidence on urgent care red flags indicates that urgent evaluation is needed for a lump that is hard, fixed, painless, growing, or lasting beyond 3 to 4 weeks, especially if there are other concerning symptoms such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The patient should not delay care if they are worried or if the lump is painful. In this case, the provider’s advice to seek care is consistent with the evidence that not all lumps are cancerous and that evaluation is needed to rule out serious issues [N1-R3][N1-R4]. So the next steps are: explain the situation clearly, ask for a thorough evaluation and explanation, and follow up promptly if the provider is not available.

Best estimate of whether the lump is serious or not

The evidence suggests that a painful lump is more likely to be benign than cancerous, but evaluation is still needed to be sure. The breast-lump literature states that “most” palpable breast lumps are benign, and breast cancer is diagnosed in only about 10% of new breast lumps [N1-F1]. For a general lump, the same logic applies: many lumps are benign, including cysts, infections, and other non-cancerous growths, and the main concern is to distinguish those from cancer [N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. However, the evidence also emphasizes that evaluation is essential because some lumps may still be malignant and should be investigated rather than assumed benign [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Red flags that would suggest more urgent evaluation include a hard, fixed, painless, growing lump or one lasting beyond 3 to 4 weeks, especially with fever, night sweats, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The urgent-care policy also notes that severe pain, active bleeding, chest pain, shortness of breath, or altered mental status are red flags that require immediate attention [N2-F2]. For a painful lump, the most important red flags are whether it is hard, fixed, growing, or has been present for more than a few weeks, and whether it is associated with systemic symptoms [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Pain itself does not make a lump automatically serious, but it can be part of a concerning pattern if the lump is not soft, movable, or stable.

What kind of provider assessment is usually needed depends on the location of the lump, but the evidence points to a standard approach involving history, physical exam, imaging, and, when needed, biopsy [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R4]. The triple assessment for breast lumps includes a history and physical examination, breast imaging, and a biopsy if needed [N1-F1]. For non-breast lumps, the evidence supports a similar pattern: a provider will examine the lump, take a detailed history, and may order imaging to determine whether further investigation is needed [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2]. So the usual assessment is not limited to a single test but includes a combination of history, exam, and imaging.

Pain and duration both affect urgency. Pain alone is not necessarily urgent, but a painful lump that is hard, fixed, or growing may be more concerning, especially if it is not typical of a benign cyst or infection [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Duration matters because a lump lasting longer than a few weeks may be more worrisome than a new or short-lived one [N2-R1]. The evidence also says that some lumps should be evaluated promptly rather than waiting for a non-urgent referral, especially if they are unexplained and painful [N2-R4]. Overall, the lump is not automatically serious, but it is serious enough to warrant evaluation, and the urgency depends on the lump’s hardness, mobility, growth, and associated symptoms [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-F2].

Common non-cancerous causes of lumps and how to interpret them

The most common benign causes of lumps are cysts, infections, and other non-cancerous growths such as lipomas, ganglion cysts, sebaceous cysts, epidermoid cysts, dermatofibromas, and abscesses [N4-F4][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that many lumps are not connected to the immune system and can develop due to blocked glands, infection, trauma, or chronic conditions [N4-R3]. In the context of a painful lump, the most important non-cancerous interpretations are infections and inflammatory conditions, because those can cause pain and swelling [N4-R5].

Infections often present as painful, swollen lumps, and may be accompanied by redness, warmth, or fever [N4-R5]. Cysts are closed sacs of tissue and are typically not painful unless they become infected, inflamed, or ruptured [N4-R1][N4-R3]. Ganglion cysts are hard, non-cancerous bumps, often near joints or tendons, and may be associated with trauma or repetitive motion [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Lipomas are fatty growths that are usually soft, movable, and painless, but they can be painful if they are located in a tense area or are compressed [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Dermatofibromas are firm, skin-colored bumps that can be painful when pressed [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Abscesses are painful, swollen, and often red, and they are usually caused by infection [N4-R4].

What to avoid assuming is that any painful lump is cancerous. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that many lumps are benign and that evaluation is needed to rule out cancer rather than assume it [N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. What to ask for confirmation is whether the lump is likely benign, whether it is moving, whether it has changed in size or shape, and whether tests are needed to be sure [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The patient should also ask whether the lump is hard, fixed, or growing, because those features are more concerning and may point to a need for urgent evaluation [N2-R1][N2-F2]. In short, the evidence supports a practical interpretation: pain and swelling can often be explained by infection, cysts, trauma, or other benign conditions, but those explanations should not prevent a careful evaluation [N4-F4][N4-R5].

Options for care access without insurance

The strongest practical options for care without insurance are local clinics and community health centers, which are explicitly designed to provide services on a sliding scale or low-cost basis [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence from one clinic page shows that a sliding fee discount program provides reduced rates for those who qualify, and the clinic accepts Medicare and HUSKY Health (Medicaid) as well as many commercial plans [N3-F3]. That means uninsured patients can still get care at these sites, often with fees adjusted by income and household size [N3-R1][N3-F3]. Another clinic page notes that uninsured patients can be connected with eligibility assistance and that the Access to Care team can help determine insurance eligibility and apply for coverage [N3-F3]. This is particularly helpful for patients who are not sure whether they qualify for insurance or how to enroll.

Sliding-scale pricing and payment arrangements are available in several ways. The evidence shows that patients who qualify for a sliding fee discount pay reduced rates, and the program can also be applied to insurance deductibles for insured patients [N3-R4][N3-F3]. Payment can be made with cash, checks, money orders, or major credit cards, and there are options for walk-in, phone, and online payments [N3-F3]. The clinic also offers payment plans for unpaid balances, which is important for patients who cannot pay upfront [N3-F3]. The evidence also supports that some clinics offer a 40% discount on bills for uninsured or underinsured patients [N6-R3], and that financial assistance programs can help low-income, uninsured, or underinsured patients pay for all or part of medical care [N6-R1]. Mayo Clinic’s financial advocacy service is also relevant because it helps patients without insurance navigate billing and payment [N6-R5].

How to find nearby affordable services depends on the patient’s location, but the evidence gives several practical routes. The community health center page says to look for local clinics and community health centers and to contact the Access to Care team [N3-F3]. The federal health center page also explains that patients can get free or low-cost care at community health centers even with no insurance [N3-R2]. The local clinic page provides a specific example of eligibility assistance and sliding-scale fee information [N3-F3]. If the patient cannot afford a visit upfront, the evidence supports asking about sliding-scale discounts, payment plans, and financial assistance programs [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3]. In short, the best approach is to contact a local clinic or community health center, explain insurance status, and ask for sliding-scale pricing, financial assistance, or payment plan options [N3-R2][N3-F3][N6-R1].

## Final answer: Is the lump serious?

Based on the evidence provided, the short answer is **probably not serious**, but **evaluation is still needed** to be sure. Many lumps are benign, and the most common causes include cysts, infections, lipomas, ganglion cysts, and other non-cancerous growths [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4][N4-F4]. The evidence also says that not all lumps are cancerous and that a healthcare professional should evaluate any new or concerning lump [N1-F1][N1-R3]. So the lump is likely benign, but the best approach is to get a proper assessment rather than assume it is cancerous [N1-R3][N1-R4].

## 1) Likelihood that the lump is cancerous versus benign

The strongest evidence is that **most lumps are benign**, and **breast cancer is diagnosed in only about 10% of new breast lumps** [N1-F1]. For general lumps, the same logic applies: many are not cancerous, and the main purpose of evaluation is to distinguish benign from malignant causes [N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. The evidence also emphasizes that a provider will typically use a history and physical exam, imaging, and sometimes a biopsy to evaluate a lump [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R4]. That means the lump is not automatically cancerous, but it needs to be checked carefully.

## 2) When the lump might be more serious

The evidence suggests that the lump becomes more concerning if it has **hard, fixed, painless, growing features**, or if it lasts **more than 3 to 4 weeks**, especially when combined with **fever, night sweats, weight loss**, or other systemic symptoms [N2-R1][N2-F2]. In this case, the patient says the lump is **painful**, which is not itself a red flag for cancer, but it does mean the provider should pay close attention to whether the lump is hard, fixed, or growing [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Pain alone is not enough to conclude seriousness, but it can be part of a concerning pattern [N2-R1].

## 3) What kind of provider assessment is usually needed

A typical provider assessment includes a **history and physical exam**, and often **imaging** such as ultrasound or mammogram, with **biopsy** used when needed [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R4]. The evidence also notes that the provider may order imaging and biopsies to help distinguish benign from malignant causes [N1-R2][N1-R4]. For non-breast lumps, the same pattern applies: a provider will examine the lump, take a detailed history, and may use imaging to decide whether further testing is needed [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2]. So the usual assessment is not limited to a single test, but is a combination of history, exam, and imaging.

## 4) How pain and duration affect urgency

Pain alone is not enough to make the lump urgent, but **pain plus hard, fixed, growing, or long-lasting features** raises concern [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The evidence also says that some lumps should be evaluated promptly rather than waiting for a non-urgent referral, especially if they are unexplained and painful [N2-R4]. In this case, because the patient is worried and the lump is painful, the best course is to **see a provider soon**, rather than wait for a later appointment [N2-F2][N1-F1].

## 5) Practical reassurance for the patient

The provider’s advice is correct: a lump does not automatically mean cancer, and many lumps are benign [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The patient should explain the situation clearly to a provider by saying something like, “I found a lump that hurts, and I’m worried it might be something serious. I want to know what it could be and what I should do next” [N1-F1][N2-F2]. During the evaluation, the patient should ask whether the lump is likely cancerous, whether more tests are needed, and what the results would mean [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The provider may also explain whether the lump is moving, whether it has changed in size or shape, and whether any red flags exist [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 6) What to avoid assuming and what to ask for confirmation

Do **not** assume the lump is cancerous. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that many lumps are benign and that evaluation is needed to rule out cancer rather than assume it [N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. What you should ask for confirmation is:  
- Is this likely to be benign?  
- What are the next steps?  
- Do I need imaging or a biopsy?  
- What features would make this more serious?  
- What should I do if I can’t afford a visit? [N1-F1][N1-R2][N2-F2][N3-F3]

## 7) What the provider should do next

The provider should start with a history and physical exam, and then decide whether imaging or other tests are needed [N1-F1][N1-R2]. If the lump is worrisome, the provider may also refer the patient for urgent care or a specialist evaluation [N2-F2]. If the provider is unavailable, the patient should follow up as soon as possible, because delayed care can be harmful if the lump has concerning features [N2-F2].

## 8) Options for care without insurance

The strongest practical options are **local clinics and community health centers**, which offer services on a **sliding scale or low-cost basis** [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence shows that clinics can provide reduced rates for uninsured patients, and some offer a **sliding fee discount program** based on income and household size [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-F3]. Payment options include cash, checks, money orders, and major credit cards, with the possibility of **payment plans** for unpaid balances [N3-F3]. Other options include financial assistance programs, which can help low-income, uninsured, or underinsured patients pay for care [N6-R1]. In short, the patient does **not** have to go without care because of lack of insurance [N3-R2][N6-R1].

## 9) Next steps for the patient

To summarize:  
- Explain clearly to a provider: “I found a lump that hurts, and I’m worried it might be something serious.” [N1-F1][N2-F2]  
- Ask for a thorough evaluation and explanation.  
- Ask whether the lump is likely cancerous, what tests are needed, and what the results would mean [N1-F1][N1-R2].  
- If the provider is unavailable, follow up as soon as possible [N2-F2].  
- If insurance is a problem, look into local clinics, community health centers, sliding-scale discounts, payment plans, or financial assistance [N3-R2][N3-F3][N6-R1].

## Bottom line

The lump is **probably not serious**, but it is **definitely serious enough to evaluate**. The evidence supports that many lumps are benign and that painful lumps are more likely benign than cancerous [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. At the same time, the provider should not dismiss the patient’s worry, because some features — such as hardness, fixity, growth, or long duration — can point to a more serious issue [N2-R1][N2-F2]. So the best answer is: **not automatically serious, but definitely not something to ignore**. Go see a provider soon, and do not delay care if the lump becomes more concerning [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Practical reassurance and next steps for the patient

The best way to explain the situation clearly to a provider is to say: “I found a lump that hurts, and I’m worried it might be something serious. I want to know what it could be and what I should do next.” That is direct, honest, and gives the provider enough context to ask focused questions. The evidence supports that most lumps are benign and that evaluation is usually needed to distinguish benign from malignant causes [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. It also suggests that a provider will ask about the lump’s characteristics, duration, and any changes, which helps build a clearer picture of what is happening [N1-F1].

During the evaluation, the patient should ask for the provider to explain whether the lump is likely cancerous or not, and whether more tests are needed [N1-F1]. The evidence also says that a provider may order imaging and biopsies when necessary, so it is reasonable to ask, “What tests will you do?” and “What do those results mean?” [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The patient should also ask about whether the lump is moving, whether it has changed in size or shape, and whether there are any red flags that would require urgent care [N2-R1][N2-F2]. A practical next step is to ask the provider to explain the findings in plain language and to clarify whether follow-up is needed.

If the provider is unavailable, the patient should follow up as soon as possible. The evidence on urgent care red flags indicates that urgent evaluation is needed for a lump that is hard, fixed, painless, growing, or lasting beyond 3 to 4 weeks, especially if there are other concerning symptoms such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The patient should not delay care if they are worried or if the lump is painful. In this case, the provider’s advice to seek care is consistent with the evidence that not all lumps are cancerous and that evaluation is needed to rule out serious issues [N1-R3][N1-R4]. So the next steps are: explain the situation clearly, ask for a thorough evaluation and explanation, and follow up promptly if the provider is not available.

Best estimate of whether the lump is serious or not

The evidence suggests that a painful lump is more likely to be benign than cancerous, but evaluation is still needed to be sure. The breast-lump literature states that “most” palpable breast lumps are benign, and breast cancer is diagnosed in only about 10% of new breast lumps [N1-F1]. For a general lump, the same logic applies: many lumps are benign, including cysts, infections, and other non-cancerous growths, and the main concern is to distinguish those from cancer [N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. However, the evidence also emphasizes that evaluation is essential because some lumps may still be malignant and should be investigated rather than assumed benign [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Red flags that would suggest more urgent evaluation include a hard, fixed, painless, growing lump or one lasting beyond 3 to 4 weeks, especially with fever, night sweats, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The urgent-care policy also notes that severe pain, active bleeding, chest pain, shortness of breath, or altered mental status are red flags that require immediate attention [N2-F2]. For a painful lump, the most important red flags are whether it is hard, fixed, growing, or has been present for more than a few weeks, and whether it is associated with systemic symptoms [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Pain itself does not make a lump automatically serious, but it can be part of a concerning pattern if the lump is not soft, movable, or stable.

What kind of provider assessment is usually needed depends on the location of the lump, but the evidence points to a standard approach involving history, physical exam, imaging, and, when needed, biopsy [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R4]. The triple assessment for breast lumps includes a history and physical examination, breast imaging, and a biopsy if needed [N1-F1]. For non-breast lumps, the evidence supports a similar pattern: a provider will examine the lump, take a detailed history, and may order imaging to determine whether further investigation is needed [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2]. So the usual assessment is not limited to a single test but includes a combination of history, exam, and imaging.

Pain and duration both affect urgency. Pain alone is not necessarily urgent, but a painful lump that is hard, fixed, or growing may be more concerning, especially if it is not typical of a benign cyst or infection [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Duration matters because a lump lasting longer than a few weeks may be more worrisome than a new or short-lived one [N2-R1]. The evidence also says that some lumps should be evaluated promptly rather than waiting for a non-urgent referral, especially if they are unexplained and painful [N2-R4]. Overall, the lump is not automatically serious, but it is serious enough to warrant evaluation, and the urgency depends on the lump’s hardness, mobility, growth, and associated symptoms [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-F2].

Common non-cancerous causes of lumps and how to interpret them

The most common benign causes of lumps are cysts, infections, and other non-cancerous growths such as lipomas, ganglion cysts, sebaceous cysts, epidermoid cysts, dermatofibromas, and abscesses [N4-F4][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that many lumps are not connected to the immune system and can develop due to blocked glands, infection, trauma, or chronic conditions [N4-R3]. In the context of a painful lump, the most important non-cancerous interpretations are infections and inflammatory conditions, because those can cause pain and swelling [N4-R5].

Infections often present as painful, swollen lumps, and may be accompanied by redness, warmth, or fever [N4-R5]. Cysts are closed sacs of tissue and are typically not painful unless they become infected, inflamed, or ruptured [N4-R1][N4-R3]. Ganglion cysts are hard, non-cancerous bumps, often near joints or tendons, and may be associated with trauma or repetitive motion [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Lipomas are fatty growths that are usually soft, movable, and painless, but they can be painful if they are located in a tense area or are compressed [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Dermatofibromas are firm, skin-colored bumps that can be painful when pressed [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Abscesses are painful, swollen, and often red, and they are usually caused by infection [N4-R4].

What to avoid assuming is that any painful lump is cancerous. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that many lumps are benign and that evaluation is needed to rule out cancer rather than assume it [N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. What to ask for confirmation is whether the lump is likely benign, whether it is moving, whether it has changed in size or shape, and whether tests are needed to be sure [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The patient should also ask whether the lump is hard, fixed, or growing, because those features are more concerning and may point to a need for urgent evaluation [N2-R1][N2-F2]. In short, the evidence supports a practical interpretation: pain and swelling can often be explained by infection, cysts, trauma, or other benign conditions, but those explanations should not prevent a careful evaluation [N4-F4][N4-R5].

Options for care access without insurance

The strongest practical options for care without insurance are local clinics and community health centers, which are explicitly designed to provide services on a sliding scale or low-cost basis [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence from one clinic page shows that a sliding fee discount program provides reduced rates for those who qualify, and the clinic accepts Medicare and HUSKY Health (Medicaid) as well as many commercial plans [N3-F3]. That means uninsured patients can still get care at these sites, often with fees adjusted by income and household size [N3-R1][N3-F3]. Another clinic page notes that uninsured patients can be connected with eligibility assistance and that the Access to Care team can help determine insurance eligibility and apply for coverage [N3-F3]. This is particularly helpful for patients who are not sure whether they qualify for insurance or how to enroll.

Sliding-scale pricing and payment arrangements are available in several ways. The evidence shows that patients who qualify for a sliding fee discount pay reduced rates, and the program can also be applied to insurance deductibles for insured patients [N3-R4][N3-F3]. Payment can be made with cash, checks, money orders, or major credit cards, and there are options for walk-in, phone, and online payments [N3-F3]. The clinic also offers payment plans for unpaid balances, which is important for patients who cannot pay upfront [N3-F3]. The evidence also supports that some clinics offer a 40% discount on bills for uninsured or underinsured patients [N6-R3], and that financial assistance programs can help low-income, uninsured, or underinsured patients pay for all or part of medical care [N6-R1]. Mayo Clinic’s financial advocacy service is also relevant because it helps patients without insurance navigate billing and payment [N6-R5].

How to find nearby affordable services depends on the patient’s location, but the evidence gives several practical routes. The community health center page says to look for local clinics and community health centers and to contact the Access to Care team [N3-F3]. The federal health center page also explains that patients can get free or low-cost care at community health centers even with no insurance [N3-R2]. The local clinic page provides a specific example of eligibility assistance and sliding-scale fee information [N3-F3]. If the patient cannot afford a visit upfront, the evidence supports asking about sliding-scale discounts, payment plans, and financial assistance programs [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3]. The strongest evidence is that **most lumps are benign**, and **breast cancer is diagnosed in only about 10% of new breast lumps** [N1-F1]. That means the lump is not automatically cancerous, but it needs to be checked carefully.

## 2) When the lump might be more serious

The evidence suggests that the lump becomes more concerning if it has **hard, fixed, painless, growing features**, or if it lasts **more than 3 to 4 weeks**, especially when combined with **fever, night sweats, weight loss**, or other systemic symptoms [N2-R1][N2-F2]. In this case, the patient says the lump is **painful**, which is not itself a red flag for cancer, but it does mean the provider should pay close attention to whether the lump is hard, fixed, or growing [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Pain alone is not enough to conclude seriousness, but it can be part of a concerning pattern [N2-R1].
